topics.title: Weather, climate and the monsoon type

learn.hook: A rainy afternoon in Pune is weather. Pune's pattern of wet summers and dry winters, year after year, is its climate.
points: Weather is the momentary state of the atmosphere; climate is the average of weather conditions over a long period of time (more than thirty years).
Weather changes quickly, within a day or a week, while climate changes very slowly and may be noticed only after many years.
The elements of weather and climate are temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind, humidity and precipitation.
India has a 'monsoon' type of climate, which is found mainly in South and South-east Asia.
The monsoon regime emphasises the unity of India with the rest of South-east Asia, even though there are many regional variations within India.

example.q: Classify: (a) 'It is 39°C and humid in Chennai today'; (b) 'Chennai gets most of its rain in October–November every year'.
steps: (a) describes the state of the atmosphere at one moment → weather.
(b) describes the long-term average pattern → climate.

topics.title: Diversity within India's monsoon climate and Koeppen's regions

learn.hook: On the same winter night, Drass in Ladakh can drop to −45°C while Thiruvananthapuram stays at 22°C.
points: Temperature varies greatly: in summer, the Rajasthan desert may reach about 50°C while Pahalgam in Kashmir is around 20°C. On a winter night, Drass may be as low as −45°C while Thiruvananthapuram has 22°C.

Precipitation varies in form and amount: snowfall occurs in the Himalaya while the rest of India gets rain. Cherrapunji and Mawsynram in the Khasi hills receive over 1,080 cm a year, while Jaisalmer rarely gets more than 9 cm.
Seasons differ: most of India gets rain from June to September, but the Tamil Nadu coast gets most of its rain in October and November (early winter).
Differences in winds, temperature, rainfall, the rhythm of seasons and the degree of wetness or dryness create regional diversity within the overall monsoon unity.

Koeppen's scheme for India: Amw (west coast south of Goa), As (Coromandel coast of Tamil Nadu), Aw (most of the Peninsular plateau south of the Tropic of Cancer), BShw (north-western Gujarat, parts of western Rajasthan and Punjab), BWhw (extreme western Rajasthan), Cwg (Ganga plain, eastern Rajasthan, northern Madhya Pradesh, most of the North-east), Dfc (Arunachal Pradesh), E (Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand).

topics.title: Factors determining India's climate: location and relief

learn.hook: Agra and Darjeeling lie at almost the same latitude, yet in January Agra averages about 16°C and Darjeeling only about 4°C.
points: Latitude: the Tropic of Cancer passes through the middle of India; the area south of it is tropical and the area north of it is subtropical (warm temperate), with greater extremes of temperature.
The Himalaya act as an effective climatic divide: they protect the subcontinent from cold northern winds and trap the monsoon winds, forcing them to shed their moisture within the subcontinent.

Distribution of land and water: India is flanked by the Indian Ocean on three sides in the south and a high, continuous mountain wall in the north. Land and water heat and cool differently, creating different air pressure zones in different seasons, which causes the reversal of monsoon winds.

Distance from the sea: coastal areas have an equable or maritime climate; interior areas far from the sea's moderating influence have extreme climates (continentality), e.g. Delhi, Kanpur and Amritsar.

Altitude: temperature decreases with height (Agra 16°C vs Darjeeling 4°C in January). Relief affects temperature, pressure, wind direction and speed and rainfall: windward slopes of the Western Ghats and Assam get heavy rain, while the southern plateau in their rain shadow stays dry.

example.q: Why is Mumbai's climate more equable than Delhi's?
steps: Mumbai is on the coast; the sea heats and cools slowly.

So Mumbai has a smaller temperature range.
example.answer: Because of distance from the sea: Mumbai is maritime, Delhi is continental.

topics.title: Pressure, winds and jet streams in winter

learn.hook: January snow in Kashmir and winter showers in Punjab are delivered by storms that began over the Mediterranean Sea, carried by a river of fast wind high in the sky.
points: Three factors related to air pressure and winds shape India's climate: (i) the distribution of air pressure and winds on the earth's surface; (ii) upper air circulation, caused by global weather controls and the inflow of different air masses and jet streams; (iii) the inflow of western cyclones (disturbances) in winter and tropical depressions in the south-west monsoon period.

In winter, weather is governed by pressure in Central and Western Asia. A high-pressure centre develops to the north of the Himalaya, and dry continental winds blow from it towards the low pressure over the oceans to the south; in north-western India these winds meet the trade winds.

Jet streams: in winter, Western and Central Asia lie under westerly winds blowing at 9–13 km from west to east. The Tibetan highlands act as a barrier and split this jet stream into two branches: one north of the Tibetan highlands and a southern branch blowing eastward south of the Himalaya, over India (mean position in February about 25°N).

Western cyclonic disturbances enter India from the west and north-west in winter. They originate over the Mediterranean Sea and are brought into India by the westerly jet stream; a rise in night temperature generally signals their approach.

Tropical cyclones originate over the Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean (mainly October–December). With very high winds and heavy rain, they hit the Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha coasts and are very destructive.

topics.title: Summer mechanism: ITCZ, monsoon trough and the easterly jet

learn.hook: By mid-July, a band of low pressure stretches across the Ganga plain. Winds from as far as the Southern Hemisphere rush towards it, and that rush is our monsoon.
points: The Inter Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) is a low-pressure zone at the equator where trade winds converge, so air tends to rise there. In July it lies around 20°N–25°N over the Gangetic plain and is sometimes called the monsoon trough. It encourages a thermal low over north and north-west India.

Due to the shift of the ITCZ, the trade winds of the Southern Hemisphere cross the equator between 40°E and 60°E and, deflected by the Coriolis force, blow from south-west to north-east: the south-west monsoon. In winter the ITCZ moves south and winds reverse, blowing from the north-east: the north-east monsoon.

By the middle of July the westerly jet stream withdraws from the Indian region. An easterly jet stream flows over the southern Peninsula in June (maximum speed about 90 km/h); in August it is confined to about 15°N and in September to about 22°N.
The easterly jet stream steers tropical depressions into India. These depressions play a big role in distributing monsoon rain; their tracks are the areas of highest rainfall in India.

'Monsoon' means a seasonal reversal in wind direction. Our understanding of it has grown through observations from ships and aircraft, satellite data and research programmes such as the Monsoon Experiment (MONEX).

example.q: Why do the south-east trade winds become south-west monsoon winds after crossing the equator?
steps: The ITCZ shifts north to about 20°N–25°N in summer.
The trades of the Southern Hemisphere are drawn across the equator towards it.
North of the equator the Coriolis force deflects winds to the right.
So south-east trades turn into south-westerly winds: the south-west monsoon.
example.answer: Because the Coriolis force deflects them to the right after they cross the equator.

topics.title: Onset of the monsoon, El Nino and the Southern Oscillation

learn.hook: Every year around 1 June, all of India watches Kerala. When the monsoon arrives there, it races north to cover the country within about six weeks.
points: The classical explanation (going back to Edmond Halley) is differential heating of land and sea. In April–May, when the sun shines vertically over the Tropic of Cancer, the large landmass north of the Indian Ocean is intensely heated, creating an intense low over north-western India and Pakistan, while the ocean to the south stays at higher pressure. This thermal low pulls in the south-east trades across the equator.

The south-west monsoon is thus a continuation of the south-east trades, deflected towards India after crossing the equator (between 40°E and 60°E). The northward shift of the ITCZ is linked with the withdrawal of the westerly jet stream; the easterly jet that sets in along 15°N after this is held responsible for the burst of the monsoon.
Onset: the south-west monsoon sets in over the Kerala coast by about 1 June, reaches Mumbai and Kolkata between about 10 and 13 June, and by mid-July covers the entire subcontinent.

El Nino is a warm current that appears off the coast of Peru in some years (once every three to seven years), replacing the cold Peruvian (Humboldt) current and raising water temperature by about 10°C. It distorts equatorial atmospheric circulation, causes irregular evaporation of sea water and reduces plankton (and fish). The name means 'Child Christ' as it appears around Christmas. India uses it for long-range monsoon forecasting.

Southern Oscillation (SO): normally, when the tropical eastern South Pacific has high pressure, the tropical eastern Indian Ocean has low pressure; in some years this reverses. The pressure difference between Tahiti (Pacific) and Darwin (northern Australia) is used to predict monsoon intensity; a negative difference suggests below-average and late monsoons. El Nino and SO together are ENSO.

topics.title: Monsoon arrival, rain-bearing systems, burst and breaks

learn.hook: Mumbai's first monsoon downpour, with thunder and lightning, can drop the temperature by several degrees in an hour. That's the 'burst'.
points: By early June the low pressure over north-western India becomes powerful enough to attract the trade winds of the Southern Hemisphere. Crossing the equator and passing over warm waters, they bring abundant moisture; following a south-westerly direction, they are the south-west monsoon.

Rain begins abruptly. The sudden onset of moisture-laden winds with violent thunder and lightning is called the 'burst' of the monsoon. It may come in the first week of June on the coasts of Kerala, Karnataka, Goa and Maharashtra, but be delayed to the first week of July in the interior. Day temperatures fall by 5°C–8°C between mid-June and mid-July. The monsoon covers the country in about a month.
The monsoon approaches the landmass in two branches: the Arabian Sea branch and the Bay of Bengal branch.

Two rain-bearing systems: the first originates in the Bay of Bengal (tropical depressions) and brings rain to the plains of north India; the second is the Arabian Sea current, which brings rain to the west coast. Rain on the Western Ghats is mostly orographic; its intensity depends on offshore meteorological conditions and the position of the equatorial jet stream along East Africa. The paths of Bay of Bengal depressions are set by the position of the monsoon trough, whose axis oscillates.

A break in the monsoon is when rain fails for one or more weeks after a few rainy days. In northern India, breaks occur when rain-bearing storms are infrequent along the monsoon trough (ITCZ); on the west coast, dry spells occur when winds blow parallel to the coast.

example.q: Why might the Konkan coast have a dry week in the middle of July?
steps: West-coast rain needs moist winds blowing onto the Western Ghats.

So a dry spell (break) occurs.

topics.title: Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches; nature of monsoon rainfall

learn.hook: Mawsynram, on the crest of the Khasi hills, receives the highest average annual rainfall in the world, while the Tamil Nadu coast stays fairly dry in the same season.
points: Arabian Sea branch splits into three: (i) one is obstructed by the Western Ghats; climbing to 900–1,200 m, it gives the windward Sahyadri and west coastal plain 250–400 cm of rain, then descends and warms, leaving a rain-shadow east of the Ghats; (ii) another strikes the coast north of Mumbai, moves along the Narmada and Tapi valleys into central India (the Chotanagpur plateau gets about 15 cm from it) and joins the Bay of Bengal branch in the Ganga plains; (iii) a third strikes Saurashtra and Kachchh, passes over west Rajasthan along the Aravali with scanty rain, and joins the Bay of Bengal branch in Punjab and Haryana. Together they bring rain to the western Himalaya.

Bay of Bengal branch strikes Myanmar and south-east Bangladesh; the Arakan Hills deflect much of it towards India, so it enters West Bengal and Bangladesh from the south and south-east. It splits: one branch moves west along the Ganga plains up to Punjab; the other moves up the Brahmaputra valley, giving widespread rain; a sub-branch strikes the Garo and Khasi hills, where Mawsynram gets the world's highest average annual rainfall.
The Tamil Nadu coast stays dry in this season because (i) it lies parallel to the Bay of Bengal branch and (ii) it is in the rain shadow of the Arabian Sea branch.

Characteristics of monsoon rainfall: seasonal (June–September); largely governed by relief (over 250 cm on the windward Ghats); declining with distance from the sea (Kolkata about 119 cm, Patna 105 cm, Allahabad 76 cm, Delhi 56 cm in the season); wet spells interrupted by breaks; heavy downpours causing runoff and soil erosion; over three-fourths of India's rain comes in this season; uneven spatial distribution (12 cm to over 250 cm); and uncertain onset and withdrawal.

learn.hook: In January, Punjab may shiver near freezing at night while Thiruvananthapuram enjoys a balmy 31°C afternoon. The cold season is a northern story.
points: Meteorologists recognise four seasons: the cold weather season, the hot weather season, the south-west monsoon season and the retreating monsoon season.

The cold weather season begins from mid-November in northern India and lasts till February; December and January are the coldest months in the northern plain. Mean daily temperature stays below 21°C over most of northern India; nights can go below freezing in Punjab and Rajasthan. Reasons: distance from the sea (continental climate), snowfall in the nearby Himalaya creating cold waves, and cold winds from the Caspian Sea and Turkmenistan bringing cold waves, frost and fog around February.

Temperature decreases from south to north. The Peninsula has no well-defined cold season because of the sea's moderating influence and nearness to the equator; e.g. Thiruvananthapuram's mean maximum is about 31°C in January and 29.5°C in June.

Pressure and winds: feeble high pressure over the northern plain and slightly lower pressure in the south; light winds (3–5 km/h) blow outward from the north-west, westerly or north-westerly down the Ganga valley, northerly in the delta and north-easterly over the Bay of Bengal. Winter monsoon winds generally do not cause rain because they blow from land to sea and carry little moisture.

Exceptions: weak temperate cyclones from the Mediterranean (western disturbances) give rain in Punjab, Haryana, Delhi and western UP; though meagre, it is very useful for rabi crops (the winter rain known locally as 'mahawat'), and falls as snow in the lower Himalaya, sustaining summer river flow. This rain decreases from west to east in the plains. In October–November, the north-east monsoon picks up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and gives torrential rain to the Tamil Nadu coast, southern Andhra Pradesh, south-east Karnataka and south-east Kerala.

topics.title: The hot weather season and its local storms

learn.hook: Mango showers ripen Kerala's mangoes, blossom showers bring out coffee flowers, and Bengal's Kalbaisakhi storms help tea, jute and rice. Summer storms have names and jobs!
points: With the sun's apparent northward movement towards the Tropic of Cancer in March, temperatures rise in north India; April, May and June are summer months there. In March the highest temperature, about 38°C, is on the Deccan Plateau; in April, 38°C–43°C in Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh; in May the heat belt moves north, and in north-west India temperatures around 48°C are not uncommon.
The hot season in south India is milder because of the moderating ocean: temperatures stay between 26°C and 32°C. Due to altitude, the hills of the Western Ghats remain below 25°C.

Pressure and winds: excessive heat and falling pressure in the north. The ITCZ moves north, centred at about 25°N in July; the monsoon trough extends from the Thar desert to Patna and the Chotanagpur plateau. In the north-west, hot, dry winds called 'loo' blow in the afternoon, often into midnight. Evening dust storms are common in May in Punjab, Haryana, eastern Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.

Local storms: (i) Mango shower: pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and coastal Karnataka that help mangoes ripen early. (ii) Blossom shower: makes coffee flowers blossom in Kerala and nearby areas. (iii) Nor'westers: dreaded evening thunderstorms in Bengal and Assam, called 'Kalbaisakhi' (calamity of the month of Baisakh) in Bengal and 'Bardoli Chheerha' in Assam; useful for tea, jute and rice. (iv) Loo: hot, dry, oppressive winds in the northern plains from Punjab to Bihar, strongest between Delhi and Patna.

topics.title: Retreating monsoon and the traditional Indian seasons

learn.hook: Ancient Indian calendars split the year into six seasons, from Vasanta to Shishira. Modern meteorologists use four, including the 'October heat' of the retreating monsoon.
points: October and November are the months of the retreating monsoon. By the end of September the south-west monsoon weakens as the low-pressure trough of the Ganga plain moves south with the sun's southward march.

The monsoon retreats from western Rajasthan by the first week of September and from Rajasthan, Gujarat, the western Ganga plain and the Central Highlands by the end of September. By early October the low pressure covers the northern Bay of Bengal, by early November it moves over Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and by mid-December it leaves the Peninsula entirely.

This season has clear skies and rising temperature while the land is still moist; the high temperature and humidity make the weather oppressive, known as 'October heat'. In the second half of October temperatures fall rapidly in the north.

The weather is dry in north India but rainy in the eastern Peninsula, where October and November are the rainiest months. Cyclonic depressions from the Andaman Sea cross the east coast; these destructive tropical cyclones target the thickly populated deltas of the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri. A bulk of the Coromandel coast's rainfall comes from these depressions and cyclones.

Traditional six seasons of two months each: Vasanta (spring, Chaitra–Vaisakha, March–April), Grishma (summer, Jyaistha–Asadha, May–June), Varsha (rainy, Sravana–Bhadra, July–August), Sharada (autumn, Asvina–Kartika, September–October), Hemanta (pre-winter, Margashirsa–Pausa, November–December) and Shishira (winter, Magha–Phalguna, January–February).

topics.title: Variability of rainfall and the monsoon as the axis of agriculture

learn.hook: In Kerala, the monsoon almost never fails; in western Rajasthan, one year can bring floods and the next a severe drought. That uncertainty is called variability.
points: Variability of rainfall is measured by the coefficient of variation: C.V. = (Standard deviation ÷ Mean) × 100. It shows how much rainfall deviates from the mean; actual rainfall in some places deviates by 20–50%.

Variability less than 25% exists on the west coast, Western Ghats, north-eastern Peninsula, eastern Ganga plains, north-east India, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and south-western Jammu and Kashmir; these areas get over 100 cm a year.

Variability over 50% exists in western Rajasthan, northern Jammu and Kashmir and the interior Deccan plateau; these areas get less than 50 cm a year. The rest of India has 25–50% variability with 50–100 cm of rain. So, generally, the lower the rainfall, the higher its variability. Map work: compare the annual rainfall map with the variability map.

The monsoon is the axis around which India's entire agricultural cycle revolves, because about 64% of people depend on agriculture for their livelihood, and agriculture itself is based on the south-west monsoon.
Except the Himalaya, all parts of India have temperatures above the threshold level for growing crops throughout the year, and regional variations in the monsoon climate help grow a variety of crops.

topics.title: Monsoon and economic life; global warming

learn.hook: A good monsoon can lift farm incomes, tractor sales and even stock markets. A failed one can mean drought, debt and higher food prices.
points: Variability of rainfall brings droughts or floods every year in some part of the country. Agricultural prosperity depends on timely and adequately distributed rain; if it fails, farming suffers, especially where irrigation is not developed.
A sudden monsoon burst causes soil erosion over large areas. Winter rainfall from temperate cyclones in north India is highly beneficial for rabi crops.
Regional climatic variation is reflected in India's vast variety of food, clothes and house types (e.g. sloping roofs in rainy regions, thick walls in hot deserts).

Global warming: climate is changing due to natural and human-induced causes. Rising greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide since the industrial revolution, are causing global warming. The mean annual surface temperature of the earth has increased over the past 150 years, and it is projected that global average temperature may rise by about 2°C by 2100.

Higher temperatures melt polar ice caps and mountain glaciers; the resulting sea-level rise would submerge coastal areas and islands such as the Maldives and low-lying deltas. Reducing emissions is a shared global concern.
